question.text: Moving Average crossovers where the 50-day MA crosses above the 200-day MA is called:

explanation.text: The Logic: In general technical-analysis terminology, a Golden Cross occurs when a short-term moving average — most commonly the 50-day MA — crosses above a long-term moving average, most commonly the 200-day MA. It is widely treated as a bullish trend-confirmation signal because the faster average rising above the slower one indicates that recent prices are trending higher than the longer-term average. The opposite event (50-day crossing below the 200-day) is called the Death Cross and is treated as bearish. The Trap: Death Cross is the bearish opposite, not the same event. Silver Cross and Diamond Cross are not recognised technical-analysis terms — they are distractors. Both correct labels (Golden / Death) refer to the same 50/200-day MA crossover, only differing in direction. Note: The specific Golden Cross / Death Cross terminology and the 50-day vs 200-day MA convention are not stated in the cited NISM Series XV Research Analyst workbook chapter on technical analysis (moving averages and Dow Theory pages checked). The framing above is general industry/technical-analysis knowledge, included here because moving-average crossovers are a standard MA application even though the named terms do not appear in the workbook.
